title: Goroutines & Channels Basics
intro: Goroutines and channels are the two features that make Go famous for concurrency, and they come up in every Go fresher interview. This module covers goroutine creation (the go keyword before a function call — that is all you need to start a new goroutine), why goroutines are lightweight (they start at about 2 KB of stack, grow dynamically, and are scheduled by the Go runtime — not the OS), the channel data type (typed conduits for communicating between goroutines), creating channels with make(chan T) for unbuffered and make(chan T, n) for buffered, sending and receiving (ch <- value to send, value := <-ch to receive), how unbuffered channels synchronise sender and receiver (both block until the other is ready), buffered channels (sender only blocks when buffer is full, receiver only blocks when buffer is empty), closing a channel (signals no more values will be sent; receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value), and ranging over a channel until it's closed. Every answer uses a runnable example and addresses the comparison: 'goroutines vs threads.'
